blocks.title: The plan and its first phases
From licence to stock on the shelf

summary.title: The end-to-end Gantt
points: Four parallel tracks: deal and dossier, regulatory, packaging and serialisation, supply.
Market access closes the loop; patents and SPCs can override the whole plan.
Only the DCP's 210 days and the 30-day national phase are fixed by law.
Everything else depends on people, partners, suppliers and printers.
Run artworks, EMVS onboarding and launch batches during the DCP, not after it.

exercises.scenario: A draft plan puts artwork, EMVS onboarding and batch planning after the national licences.

questions.prompt: What's the main problem?
options: They should run in parallel during the DCP
Nothing; those tasks legally require a national licence before they can start
EMVS onboarding isn't needed for generics
Artwork should come before the gap analysis

questions.prompt: Which segments have a legal clock?
options: The gap analysis and the artwork rounds
The DCP's 210 days and the 30-day national phase

exercises.scenario: The SPC expires six months after the expected licence.

questions.prompt: What happens to the plan?
options: Nothing; the licence date is the launch date regardless of patents
The SPC date overrides it and sets the launch

questions.prompt: Which track holds batches, EU testing and QP release?

summary.title: Phase 1: transfer and gap analysis
points: Each phase has entry criteria, work, and exit criteria.
Entry: deal signed, dossier received.
Work: inventory, gap analysis, FTO check, RMS slot, choose the EU importer.
Exit: blocking gaps closed or accepted with a plan; RMS slot confirmed.
Slips: late transfer, slow owner answers, stability or nitrosamine gaps, no RMS capacity.

exercises.scenario: Three months after signature, the dossier is in but the RMS slot isn't confirmed.

questions.prompt: Is phase 1 complete?
options: No: a confirmed RMS slot is an exit criterion
Only if the FTO is done
Yes: receiving the dossier is the only exit criterion for phase 1
Yes, if the gap analysis has started

questions.prompt: Which decision belongs in phase 1 because it goes into the dossier?
options: Choosing the EU importer and batch release site

exercises.scenario: The dossier owner says stability data 'should be ready soon'.

questions.prompt: What do you ask for?
questions.explanation: Slow answers are a classic slip.

questions.prompt: Why does phase 1 matter so much?
options: It has a fixed legal clock
It sets the earliest submission date
It replaces the DCP for in-licensed dossiers
questions.explanation: Every week saved moves the whole plan.

summary.title: Phase 2: submission and the DCP
points: Entry: dossier ready, blocking gaps closed.
Work: validation, Day 0 to 210, answering Day 105 and later questions.
Exit: end of procedure with agreed English texts.
Real length depends on clock-stops; about 7 months of assessment plus pauses.
Use clock-stops to draft artworks, start EMVS onboarding, schedule batches, prepare translations.

exercises.scenario: RA expects a 3-month clock-stop at Day 105.

questions.prompt: What should the other tracks do meanwhile?
options: Draft artworks, start EMVS onboarding, schedule batches, prepare translations
Start pricing applications in every country
Wait until the procedure ends, since texts may change during the clock-stop
questions.explanation: Often what separates fast from slow launches.

questions.prompt: What's phase 2's exit?
options: End of procedure with agreed English texts

exercises.scenario: Your plan shows phase 2 as exactly 210 days.

questions.prompt: What's missing?
options: The 60-day CMDh referral, which every DCP includes

questions.prompt: What drives the clock-stop estimate?
options: The RMS's fees and its language requirements

summary.title: Phase 3: national phase and artworks
points: Entry: texts final or near-final, with drafts started in clock-stops.
Work: translations, mock-ups, Blue Box requirements, country artwork, printed materials ordered.
Exit: national licence, approved artwork and printed materials at the packaging site, per country.
Slips: late translations, proof rounds, wrong die-line, printer capacity, a late text variation.
Each country is its own line; printed packaging gates the launch stock.

exercises.scenario: Germany has its licence and approved artwork; its cartons are still at the printer.

questions.prompt: Has Germany exited phase 3?
options: Yes: the licence and approved artwork are the only exit criteria
No: printed materials must be at the packaging site

questions.prompt: Why is each country a separate plan line?
options: Each country has its own RMS
Licence, translation, Blue Box and artwork slip independently
questions.explanation: One country's slip shouldn't hide in an average.

exercises.scenario: A text variation is approved just before cartons go to print.

questions.prompt: What's the risk?
options: Printing old texts, wasting material and delaying launch
None; variations only affect the leaflet and never the carton

questions.prompt: What gates the launch stock in phase 3?
options: The SDEA with the partner and the PSMF update
Approved artwork and printed packaging per country

summary.title: Phase 4: market access
points: Most generics only sell once priced and reimbursed, or after winning tenders.
P&R is national, with its own rules, files and timelines.
Transparency Directive maximums: 90 days price, 90 reimbursement, 180 combined.
Exit: price and status known, tender won or plan B, listed with wholesalers.
Know listing calendars; file as soon as allowed. Access can set the launch date.

exercises.scenario: A licence arrives in March; reimbursement lists are published quarterly, next in July.

questions.prompt: What's the realistic launch?
options: March, since the licence allows sales immediately in every EU country
Around the July listing, if the file is complete in time
questions.explanation: Market access, not approval, sets the date here.

questions.prompt: Who usually owns the P&R application?
options: The local market-access or commercial team, with RA support
The QP at the importing site, once stock is released

exercises.scenario: A country takes 170 days to decide both price and reimbursement together.

questions.prompt: Is that within the Transparency Directive?
options: No: the maximum is 90 days for both together
Yes: the combined maximum is 180 days
No: generics must be decided within 30 days

questions.prompt: What will the pharma reform change for these steps?
options: Bolar will explicitly allow them before patent expiry
P&R will move to the EMA

summary.title: Phase 5: EMVS readiness
points: Under the FMD, pharmacies must be able to verify every pack.
Entry: MAH known, packaging site chosen, product data defined.
Work: onboard with the EU hub, upload master data per country, set up line printing and verification.
Exit: test uploads succeed; the line prints and verifies codes.
Slips stay invisible until the first scan fails: start onboarding during the DCP.

exercises.scenario: Onboarding paperwork is planned to start after the national licences.

questions.prompt: What's the risk?
options: It takes weeks, and released packs can't be dispensed without it
None; onboarding is instant once the national licences are granted

questions.prompt: Which proves phase 5 is done?
options: Test uploads succeed and the line prints and verifies codes

exercises.scenario: One country's master data has the wrong product code.

questions.prompt: When would you normally find out without testing?
options: When the first pharmacy scan fails
questions.explanation: That's why test uploads belong on the plan.

questions.prompt: Which slip is about the packaging site?
options: A late pricing and reimbursement file in one country
The line not yet validated for serialisation

summary.title: Phase 6: launch batches to shipment
points: Entry: printed materials at the packaging site, batches scheduled.
Work: manufacture and pack, ship to the importer, full EU testing, QP certification.
Exit: released stock at the wholesaler in each country.
Launch-readiness checklist per country: licence, P&R, artwork and stock, EMVS, PV, wholesaler, communication.
Slips (deviations, documents, testing capacity) cost weeks: keep a buffer.

exercises.scenario: Stock is released, but EMVS master data for Belgium is missing.

questions.prompt: Is Belgium ready to launch?
options: No: packs would fail verification at pharmacies
Yes, if the price is set
Yes: released stock is the only condition that matters for go/no-go

questions.prompt: Which item belongs on the launch-readiness checklist?
questions.explanation: Plus licence, P&R, artwork and stock, EMVS, wholesaler, communication.

exercises.scenario: Your plan has no buffer between QP release and the launch date.

questions.prompt: Why is that risky?
What's phase 6's exit?
options: Released stock at the wholesaler in each country
Batches made and packed at the Indian site

summary.title: Critical path and slip points
points: Usual path: dossier, DCP, national texts, artwork and printing, packing, EU testing and QP, launch.
Market access, a later patent expiry or a GMP problem can take over.
Slip points: late dossier and stability gaps, long clock-stops, proof rounds and printers, documents and testing.
Watch slip points weekly, not at the end.
Re-check the critical path whenever a date moves; the Gantt explorer shows the effect.

exercises.scenario: In the reference plan, clock-stops grow from 3 to 8 months.

questions.prompt: What happens?
options: Launch moves later, because the DCP is on the critical path
Nothing, because artwork and supply run in parallel and absorb the delay
questions.explanation: No slack on the critical path.

questions.prompt: Which is a phase 3 slip point?
options: EU testing capacity for the launch batches

exercises.scenario: A country's reimbursement list moves from June to October; supply is ready in July.

questions.prompt: What happens to that country's critical path?
options: It moves back to the DCP, since texts must be re-agreed
questions.explanation: One input can switch the path.

questions.prompt: When should you re-check the critical path?
questions.explanation: It can switch at any time.

summary.title: PM toolkit (Project Kestrel)
points: RACI from the agreements: one A per row; update when roles change.
Risk register: L×I, owner, concrete action; review the top three weekly.
Decision log: what, who, when and the effect on the plan.
Kestrel: top risks at month 10 were a long clock-stop (16) and an expiring written confirmation (15); both happened.
Waiting for final texts before artwork cost Kestrel about 2 months on the critical path.

exercises.scenario: A new risk: the printer may lack capacity in Q3. Likelihood 3, impact 4.

questions.prompt: What's its score, and how is it rated?
options: 7, green, because the impact is only moderate

questions.prompt: What must the entry include?
options: The QP's name and the date of the next batch release
An owner and a concrete action

exercises.scenario: In the Kestrel RACI, the PM is R for artwork, and Labelling is A.

questions.prompt: What's the rule on A?
options: The PM is always A for every task in the plan
Two As are allowed if both teams agree

questions.prompt: Why record the 'wait for final texts' decision?
options: To make its effect on the plan visible later
Because the agency requires a decision log
To blame the person who decided
questions.explanation: So decisions aren't re-opened or forgotten.

summary.title: Capstone: a launch backwards
points: Start at the first sale, find the last gate, trace phases back, mark slips, write one lesson per phase.
Kestrel: planned month 18, first sale in Germany at month 23.
Last gate: QP release at 22.5, after the licence (19) and SPC expiry (17).
The failed batch and late EMVS data stayed inside the slack.
France launched at month 27, held by P&R, not supply.

exercises.scenario: You're walking Kestrel backwards.

questions.prompt: Which problem did not move Germany's first-sale date?
options: Import testing without a booked slot
The failed launch batch and its remake

questions.prompt: Which gate came last in Germany?

exercises.scenario: You write the lessons learned from Kestrel.

questions.prompt: Which is the best format?
options: 'Start artwork drafts at Day 105; this time they started after Day 210, costing about 2 months'

questions.prompt: What held France until month 27?
options: Late EMVS master data for the French packs

summary.title: The plan and its first phases
points: Four tracks run in parallel; only the DCP and national phase have legal clocks.
Phase 1: transfer, gap analysis, FTO, RMS slot, importer; sets the earliest submission.
Phase 2: DCP with clock-stops; use them for artwork drafts, EMVS, batches, translations.
Phase 3: translations, mock-ups, Blue Box, artwork, printed materials per country.
Entry and exit criteria show whether a phase is really done.

exercises.scenario: Month 6: the DCP is in its Day 105 clock-stop; artwork hasn't started.

questions.prompt: What's the biggest lost opportunity?
options: Booking the RMS slot, which should happen during the clock-stop

questions.prompt: What would phase 3 then risk?
options: Artwork and printing landing on the critical path
A second DCP, since the texts were agreed too late

questions.prompt: Explain entry and exit criteria, and why they help a PM.
questions.modelAnswer: Entry criteria are what must be true to start a phase; exit criteria what must be true to finish it. They stop a phase being called 'done' when key items (like a confirmed RMS slot or printed materials) are still missing.

exercises.scenario: Phase 1 is late because the dossier owner keeps promising stability data.

questions.prompt: What's the effect on the plan?
options: Nothing; the DCP can start without stability
Submission, and everything after it, moves

questions.prompt: Which phase 1 task also feeds the dossier?
options: Setting prices in each of the target countries

summary.title: From licence to stock on the shelf
points: Phase 4: P&R and tenders; national calendars can set the launch date.
Transparency Directive maximums: 90 + 90, or 180 combined.
Phase 5: EMVS onboarding, master data, line set-up; start during the DCP.
Phase 6: make, pack, ship, test, certify, deliver to wholesalers.
Go/no-go checklist per country; keep a buffer before launch.

exercises.scenario: Go/no-go meeting for three countries: A has everything; B lacks EMVS data; C awaits a July listing.

questions.prompt: Which countries can launch now?
options: A and B, since stock is released in both
questions.explanation: B fails verification; C has no listing.

questions.prompt: What sets C's date?
options: Supply, since stock is released later than the listing

questions.prompt: Name five items on a launch-readiness checklist.
questions.modelAnswer: Licence granted; price and reimbursement in place; artwork approved and stock released; EMVS live; PV system ready (also wholesaler listed, launch communication ready).

exercises.scenario: EU testing capacity is tight for the first batches.

questions.prompt: What should have been done?
options: Skip EU testing for launch stock
Ship by sea instead of by air to give the lab more time
Book the testing slot ahead of launch

questions.prompt: Which phase must be complete before serialised packs ship?

summary.title: Steering the launch
points: The critical path usually runs through the DCP, artwork and supply, but can switch.
Watch slip points weekly: gaps, clock-stops, proof rounds, documents and testing.
RACI, risk register and decision log only help if kept current.
Kestrel: planned month 18, actual 23; the last gate was released stock.
Walk launches backwards and write specific, costed lessons.

exercises.scenario: Kestrel's risk register at month 10 showed a long clock-stop (16) and an expiring written confirmation (15).

questions.prompt: What happened to both?
options: Neither happened, since they were mitigated on time

questions.prompt: Which slip ran inside the slack?
questions.explanation: It looked alarming but didn't move the date.

questions.prompt: Why did artwork drafts starting after Day 210 matter so much in Kestrel?
questions.modelAnswer: Artwork was on the critical path, so waiting for final texts instead of drafting in the clock-stop pushed printing, packing and stock, costing about 2 months.

exercises.scenario: You start a new launch next month.

questions.prompt: What do you take from Kestrel into the risk register?
options: Clock-stop length, written-confirmation expiry, EU testing slot
Only the price risk, since supply always recovers

questions.prompt: How often should the top risks be reviewed?

summary.title: Launch chronology: the whole picture
points: Four tracks in parallel; only the DCP and national phase are fixed by law.
Phases 1–6 each have entry and exit criteria.
Use clock-stops for artwork, EMVS, batches and translations.
Market access, IP or GMP can take over the critical path.
Keep RACI, risk register and decision log current; review weekly.
Walk launches backwards: last gate, slips and causes, one lesson per phase.

exercises.scenario: You plan a DCP launch in four countries with an Indian manufacturer.

questions.prompt: Which tasks run during the DCP?
options: Printing final cartons and shipping launch stock to wholesalers
Artwork drafts, EMVS onboarding, batch scheduling, translations

questions.prompt: Which phase 1 decision must be made before filing?
A country lists reimbursement twice a year. What do you do?
options: Ask the RMS to coordinate the listing with the other countries
Put its listing dates on the plan and file as soon as allowed
questions.explanation: Market access may set the date.

exercises.scenario: After launch, management asks why Kestrel launched five months late.

questions.prompt: Which chain drove it?
options: Transfer, gap closure, a long clock-stop, late artwork, packing and testing
The failed batch and the EMVS data, which both moved the date
questions.explanation: Those last ones stayed inside the slack or affected only France.

questions.prompt: Which tool showed the cost of waiting for final texts?
options: The CoA of the first launch batch

questions.prompt: Write one Kestrel lesson learned in the recommended format.
questions.modelAnswer: 'Start artwork drafts at Day 105; this time they started after Day 210, which cost about 2 months on the critical path.' (Or: 'Book the EU testing slot before the batch ships; this time it wasn't booked, costing several weeks.')
